cards.title: Iran says the Strait of Hormuz is still shut despite Trump's claims, as tanker traffic sinks to a one-week low
cards.what_happened: President Trump again insisted this week that the US has total control over the Strait of Hormuz and might 'keep it.' Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority directly contradicted that, saying the waterway remains blocked. Shipping trackers show the number of vessels transiting the strait fell to a one-week low of about **8 ships a day**, well below the recent 10-day average of around 12, and a fraction of the roughly 130 ships a day that used it before the war. Iran's Supreme National Security Council issued a list of demands before it will fully reopen the strait: the US must never threaten Iran again, end the blockade, withdraw all military assets from the region, lift sanctions, unfreeze Iranian assets, and pay compensation for war damage. Iran's foreign ministry also wants compensation specifically for pollution caused by the conflict in Gulf waters. The IEA has separately warned that global oil stockpiles are being burned through at a rapid pace as the standoff continues.
key_points: Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority insists the **Strait of Hormuz remains blocked**, contradicting repeated US claims that it has reopened.
Tracked vessel transits fell to just **8 ships a day** — the lowest since August 5 — versus roughly **130 a day** before the war started in late February.
Iran has laid out conditions to fully reopen the strait: the **US must withdraw military assets, lift sanctions, and compensate Iran** for war and environmental damage.
The **International Energy Agency** is warning that global oil stockpiles are being drawn down fast as the standoff drags on.
cards.moot: Global energy chokepoints give small countries outsized leverage over the world economy — a strait a few dozen kilometers wide can move oil prices everywhere, war or no war.

depth.background: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly **one-fifth of the world's oil and gas** normally passes through by tanker — making it one of the most important chokepoints in the global economy. Fighting between the US and Iran broke out in late February, and Iran has kept the strait effectively closed ever since, despite President Trump repeatedly insisting the US has 'total control' over it and that it's open.
depth.why_it_matters: This is a direct threat to global energy supply — every day the strait stays effectively closed, oil that would normally flow to markets doesn't, which keeps upward pressure on fuel prices worldwide and adds to inflation risk everywhere, including in oil-importing countries like India.
depth.ripple_effects: Continued low tanker traffic keeps crude oil prices elevated, raises shipping and insurance costs on alternate routes, and squeezes countries most dependent on Gulf oil imports. It also raises the odds that dwindling global oil stockpiles turn a regional standoff into a broader price shock.
depth.why_now: The IEA's fresh warning about fast-depleting oil stockpiles raises the stakes just as Iran hardens its public list of conditions, making a near-term resolution look less likely.
depth.watch_next: Whether tanker traffic through the strait recovers or falls further, and whether the US and Iran resume direct talks given the IEA's stockpile warning.
depth.market_link: Crude benchmarks and energy-linked stocks stay in focus as the standoff drags on; India, a major oil importer, faces continued pressure on the rupee and its oil import bill the longer this lasts.

key_terms.definition: A narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman that a large share of the world's traded oil and gas must pass through — one of the most important chokepoints in global energy trade.
Reserves of crude oil and refined fuel held by governments and companies as a buffer against supply disruptions; when they're drawn down quickly, prices become more sensitive to further shocks.

cards.title: China and Indonesia hold their first-ever joint navy drill east of Taiwan, and Taipei calls it a 'military provocation'
cards.what_happened: China's defence ministry said a Chinese warship and an Indonesian frigate conducted a 'passage exercise' in waters east of Taiwan in mid-August, describing it as meant to 'enhance the joint operational capabilities of the two navies' and 'jointly safeguard regional peace and stability.' It is the first time China has held a naval drill with a foreign military specifically in those waters. Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council strongly condemned the move, accusing Beijing of trying to create the false impression that China has jurisdiction over waters east of Taiwan and calling it a violation of Taiwan's sovereignty. Indonesia's navy pushed back on the framing, saying the exercise is a routine 'passing exercise' — a 'universal naval tradition' conducted while transiting another country's maritime area — as the Indonesian ship returned from a visit to Russia. Taipei Times reported the story as still developing as of August 13.
key_points: A **Chinese warship and an Indonesian frigate** are running a joint 'passage exercise' in waters **east of Taiwan** — the first time China has drilled with a foreign navy there.
Taiwan's China-policy body condemned it as **'CCP military provocation'**, saying it falsely implies China has jurisdiction over those waters.
Indonesia's navy says the drill is **routine**, calling it a standard 'passing exercise' on the way home from a port visit to **Russia**.
It's part of a broader pattern of China projecting military reach near Taiwan using **third-country partners**, not just its own fleet.
cards.moot: Sovereignty over contested waters is enforced as much through symbolism and repetition as through law — a 'routine' drill repeated enough times can quietly shift what the world treats as normal.

depth.background: Beijing claims Taiwan as its own territory and has spent years ramping up military pressure around the island — near-daily jet incursions, large-scale drills, and coast guard patrols meant to normalize a Chinese presence in disputed waters. Taiwan, a self-governing democracy of 23 million people, rejects that claim and is informally backed by the **United States**, which sells it weapons and has long signaled it would help defend the island if attacked. Indonesia is not a China ally in any formal sense — it's the world's largest Muslim-majority nation and usually prizes non-alignment — which is what makes this joint drill notable.
depth.why_it_matters: Every time China normalizes a new kind of military activity near Taiwan — this time by bringing in a foreign partner — it makes the next escalation look a little more routine. It also puts Indonesia, a country that prizes its non-aligned status, in an uncomfortable spot: seen as lending legitimacy to Chinese military activity Taiwan considers a sovereignty violation.
depth.ripple_effects: Watch for Washington and Tokyo, both of which back Taiwan's de facto autonomy, to push back diplomatically. It could also complicate Indonesia's relationships with Taiwan and with Western partners wary of Chinese military partnerships in the Indo-Pacific, and adds another data point to how markets price 'Taiwan Strait risk' — a factor that matters hugely for chipmakers like TSMC given the island's central role in global semiconductor supply.
depth.why_now: It follows months of intensifying Chinese pressure on Taiwan and comes as China has been actively courting military-cooperation partners across Asia — using a 'routine' label to make expansion of its presence harder to formally object to.
depth.watch_next: Whether Indonesia agrees to further joint drills with China near Taiwan, and how the US and Japan respond diplomatically in the coming days.
depth.market_link: Escalating China-Taiwan tension is a standing risk factor for chipmakers like TSMC and Taiwan-exposed supply chains, though this specific drill has not moved markets so far.

key_terms.definition: A relatively low-key naval drill conducted while a ship transits through or near another country's waters, often used to signal presence without a full military exercise.
Beijing's position that Taiwan is part of China, not a separate country — a claim Taiwan's government rejects.

prev_ref.title: Colombia's earthquake toll climbs as rescuers race the 72-hour survival window

cards.title: Colombia's 72-hour rescue window closes as the toll passes 220 and aid refusals spark backlash
cards.what_happened: As the **72-hour survival window** narrowed and then closed, Colombia's government confirmed it had initially declined most international rescue offers, requesting help from only the **US, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel** and stating it would rely on national rescuers instead — a marked contrast to how neighboring Venezuela accepted dozens of foreign teams without question after its own recent quakes. Colombian forensic authorities separately put the death toll at **more than 227**, above the government's own running count, while roughly **195 people remain officially listed as missing** — though volunteer-run databases estimate the real number closer to **4,000**, reflecting how hard it is to get an accurate count with damaged phone networks and blocked roads. Peru has now confirmed it will dispatch volunteers to help. Colombia's disaster-management chief defended the limited outside help, denying any ideological motive behind the decision.
key_points: The critical **72-hour survival window** for finding people alive in rubble has effectively closed, four days after the quake.
Colombia initially **limited foreign rescue offers to just four countries**, relying mainly on domestic teams — a choice now under public criticism.
Forensic authorities put the death toll at **over 227**, higher than the government's own count, with the true figure still likely rising.
**Peru** has now confirmed it will send volunteers, after Colombia widened its request for outside help.
This is being called the **first major controversy** of new president Abelardo de la Espriella's government.
cards.moot: In the first hours after a disaster, a government's choices about accepting outside help can matter as much as the disaster itself — pride or politics in a crisis window can cost lives that logistics alone wouldn't have.

thread.previously: We reported the confirmed death toll had risen to at least 224, with 700 injured and roughly 5,000 homes damaged or destroyed; Colombia's newly inaugurated president gave the first full damage briefing, and a woman was pulled alive from rubble after 30 hours.
thread.changed: The critical **72-hour survival window** — the point after which the odds of finding people alive in collapsed buildings drop sharply — has now effectively closed. It has also emerged that Colombia's government initially turned away most foreign rescue offers, asking for help from only four countries (the US, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel) and citing sole reliance on domestic rescuers — a decision now drawing criticism as the young government's first real crisis controversy.

depth.background: A **magnitude-7.4 earthquake** struck western Colombia's coffee-growing region on Sunday, August 9, and is the country's deadliest in decades. It leveled buildings across Chocó and hit hardest in Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdó, with roads into the epicenter near San José del Palmar blocked by landslides for days. The disaster landed just days into the term of Colombia's new hard-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, making it the first major crisis test of his administration.
depth.why_it_matters: The closing of the 72-hour window means rescue operations are now shifting from a race to save survivors toward recovery — while the decision to limit foreign help, made in the most critical early hours, will likely be scrutinized as a factor in how many people could still be saved.
depth.ripple_effects: The political backlash over the aid decision adds pressure on a brand-new government already managing a mass-casualty disaster, and could shape how quickly Colombia accepts international help in future emergencies. The economic cost — from destroyed homes to disrupted local businesses — will weigh on Chocó and Valle del Cauca's regional economies for months.
depth.why_now: Four days have now passed since the quake struck on August 9, pushing the disaster past the point where survival odds for anyone still trapped drop sharply — making today the natural moment the rescue-to-recovery shift becomes official.
depth.watch_next: Watch for Colombia's next official casualty update and whether the government formally opens the door to a wider range of international rescue and reconstruction assistance.

cards.title: Ukraine hits Russia's last safe Black Sea Fleet harbor at Novorossiysk, damaging four warships
cards.what_happened: Overnight on **August 12**, Ukraine's military carried out what President Zelensky called a 'unique operation' against the naval base at Novorossiysk, more than **300 kilometers** from the nearest front line. Ukrainian forces combined **Palianytsia jet-powered attack drones**, Neptune anti-ship cruise missiles, and uncrewed naval drones in the strike. Four Russian warships were damaged: the frigates **Admiral Makarov** and **Admiral Essen**, the missile ship **Buyan-M**, and the patrol ship **Vasily Bykov**. The strike also hit an S-300 air-defense radar protecting the port and the **Sheskharis oil terminal**, a major crude-export point, along with infrastructure across several piers. Russian officials have not published a detailed damage assessment.
key_points: **Four Russian warships** were damaged — two frigates (Admiral Makarov, Admiral Essen), a missile ship (Buyan-M), and a patrol ship (Vasily Bykov).
Novorossiysk sits more than **300 kilometers** from the front line and had become Russia's main safe harbor after Crimea's ports were made too dangerous.
Ukraine combined **Palianytsia jet-powered drones**, Neptune cruise missiles, and naval drones in the strike — a mix it couldn't field a few years ago.
The attack also hit the **Sheskharis oil terminal**, one of Russia's largest crude-export points, and an S-300 air-defense radar guarding the base.
President Zelensky called it a **'unique operation'** targeting what was left of Russia's Black Sea safe harbor.
cards.moot: Long-range drones let a militarily smaller country keep extending real strike pressure hundreds of kilometers past the front line — in a drone war, distance from the fighting no longer guarantees safety the way it used to.

depth.background: Novorossiysk, on Russia's Black Sea coast, became the main home of the **Black Sea Fleet** after two years of Ukrainian missile and drone strikes made Crimean ports like Sevastopol too dangerous to anchor in. The port does double duty as one of Russia's biggest oil-export terminals, moving crude that arrives via pipeline from deep inland. Through 2026, Ukraine has steadily extended the range and reliability of its domestically built long-range drones and missiles, pushing further from the front line than it could a year or two ago. This strike is the latest sign that no Russian Black Sea harbor is now truly out of reach.
depth.why_it_matters: Novorossiysk was supposed to be the safe harbor Russia's navy retreated to once Crimea's ports became too dangerous — this strike shows even that refuge is now within Ukraine's reach. It also puts a major Russian oil-export route directly in the line of fire, which matters for global crude supply.
depth.ripple_effects: Russia's Black Sea Fleet has now lost most of its historically safe anchorages, which may push it to disperse ships further east or accept that it can no longer operate safely in the western Black Sea at all. Any lasting damage to the Sheskharis terminal could disrupt Russian crude exports — a second front-line risk for oil traders already watching the separate Strait of Hormuz standoff between the US and Iran.
depth.why_now: Ukraine has spent 2026 scaling up production of longer-range drones and missiles, and Novorossiysk — long considered safely out of range — is the latest target to fall inside that expanding envelope.
depth.watch_next: Watch for satellite imagery confirming how badly the four warships and the oil terminal were damaged, and whether Russia starts relocating remaining Black Sea Fleet assets further from the coast.
depth.market_link: Any confirmed lasting damage to the Sheskharis oil terminal could tighten Russian crude exports, adding a second source of upward pressure on Brent prices alongside the separate Strait of Hormuz standoff.

key_terms.definition: The branch of Russia's navy based in the Black Sea, historically headquartered in Crimea before Ukrainian strikes forced much of it to relocate.
A Ukrainian-made jet-powered strike drone that functions like a low-cost cruise missile, used to hit targets deep inside Russia.

cards.title: An overloaded ferry capsizes on Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba, killing at least 44
cards.what_happened: A government passenger ferry that runs between the town of Kariba and surrounding islands and fishing villages capsized in choppy conditions, killing at least **44 people** so far, with search and rescue operations still ongoing for dozens more who remain missing. The vessel's rated capacity was 90 people, but it was carrying at least **114 adult passengers** plus 5 crew members and an unknown number of children when it went down — meaning it was significantly overloaded. A survivor told Zimbabwe's national broadcaster, ZBC, that passengers had pleaded with the ferry operator to turn back once the water got rough, but he refused to do so. Authorities have deployed a specialized aquatic rescue unit by air to the area, and two funeral parlors have been engaged to handle recovery of the dead.
key_points: At least **44 people have drowned** after a passenger ferry capsized on Lake Kariba, with dozens still missing.
The boat's official capacity was **90 people** — it was carrying **114 adult passengers**, 5 crew, and an unspecified number of children.
A survivor says passengers **begged the driver to turn back** because of choppy water, but he refused.
Lake Kariba is the **world's largest man-made lake** and a vital transport link for islands and fishing villages with no roads.
A specialized aquatic rescue unit was **airlifted in** to search for survivors and recover bodies.
cards.moot: Overcrowding on transport that serves communities with no alternative route is a recurring cause of mass-casualty accidents worldwide — the danger isn't usually the weather alone, it's a vessel carrying far more people than it was built to carry.

depth.background: Lake Kariba, formed by a dam on the Zambezi River, is the largest artificial lake in the world by volume, and it sits between Zimbabwe and Zambia. Because many communities on its shores and islands have no road access, government-run ferries are often the only practical way for people to travel, trade, and reach markets or hospitals. That reliance on a handful of aging vessels is exactly why overcrowding is a chronic risk on routes like this one.
depth.why_it_matters: This is one of the deadliest transport disasters in the region in years, and it exposes a familiar and preventable pattern: overcrowded, under-regulated ferries carrying people who have no safer alternative. The driver's refusal to turn back despite passenger warnings points to a systemic safety and accountability gap, not just bad weather.
depth.ripple_effects: Expect scrutiny of Zimbabwe's ferry licensing and capacity-enforcement rules, and possibly similar reviews across other Southern African countries that rely on lake and river ferries. Families in the fishing and farming communities served by this route face an immediate loss of a critical transport link on top of the human tragedy.
depth.why_now: The capsizing happened this week as the ferry was making a routine crossing in rough water, and the death toll is still rising as search teams recover more bodies and locate survivors.
depth.watch_next: Whether Zimbabwean authorities open a formal investigation into the ferry's overcrowding and the operator's decision-making, and whether the final death toll rises further.

prev_ref.title: Colombia's earthquake death toll surges past 220 as new president says 5,000 homes destroyed

cards.title: Colombia's earthquake toll climbs as rescuers race the 72-hour survival window
cards.what_happened: The quake leveled homes across Chocó, and the official death toll — verified case by case by Colombian authorities — stands at **181**, with **2,595 people injured**. Officials list **195 more as missing**, but volunteer networks tracking family reports separately estimate the true number of unaccounted-for people is closer to **4,000**, reflecting how hard it is to get an accurate count in a disaster zone with damaged phone networks and blocked roads. Search-and-rescue teams are now in a race against the **72-hour mark** since the quake struck — the rough threshold after which the odds of finding people alive in collapsed buildings drop off sharply. Rescuers still haven't been able to physically reach the epicenter near San José del Palmar because access roads are damaged or blocked by landslides.
key_points: Colombian officials confirm **at least 181 dead** and **2,595 injured** as of Wednesday's count, two days after the quake.
**195 people are officially missing**, but volunteer-run databases put the real number closer to **4,000**.
Rescue teams are racing the **72-hour survival window** — the point after which chances of finding survivors in rubble fall steeply.
Roads into the epicenter near **San José del Palmar** remain blocked, so some of the worst-hit areas still haven't been reached.
The disaster is the first major crisis test for Colombia's new president, **Abelardo de la Espriella**.
cards.moot: In disasters that hit remote, poorly connected regions, the official casualty count and the on-the-ground reality can diverge sharply for days — damaged infrastructure doesn't just kill people, it also blinds the people trying to help them.

thread.previously: We reported the magnitude-7.4 quake that hit Colombia's Chocó department had killed more than 220 people, with President Abelardo de la Espriella saying at least 5,000 homes were destroyed.
thread.changed: Colombian authorities now confirm at least 181 dead and 2,595 injured as the official count is re-verified, with 195 more listed as missing officially — though civilian-run databases put that figure closer to 4,000. Search teams are racing against the 72-hour mark after which survival chances in collapsed buildings drop sharply, and rescuers still can't reach the epicenter near San José del Palmar.

depth.background: A magnitude-7.4 earthquake struck Colombia's mountainous Chocó department on Monday, August 10, one of the strongest quakes to hit the country in decades. The region is remote and poorly connected, which is why it has taken days for rescue teams and even accurate casualty counts to reach the outside world. Colombia's government changed hands earlier this year, and this is the **first major natural disaster** the new administration has had to manage.
depth.why_it_matters: This is shaping up as one of the deadliest natural disasters in Colombia in years, and it's testing a brand-new government's ability to respond to a crisis at scale. The gap between the official missing count (195) and the civilian estimate (near 4,000) shows how much uncertainty still surrounds the true scale of the disaster.
depth.ripple_effects: Colombia will likely need significant international aid and reconstruction financing, which could strain its budget and draw in agencies like the Red Cross and UN disaster relief bodies. The remoteness of Chocó — one of Colombia's poorest regions — means rebuilding will be slow and could deepen existing inequality between it and wealthier parts of the country.
depth.why_now: Search teams are hitting the critical 72-hour survival window this week, which is why casualty figures are being revised and rescue urgency is peaking right now.
depth.watch_next: Whether rescue teams can reach the blocked-off epicenter near San José del Palmar in the next day or two, and whether the missing count converges toward the official or the civilian estimate.

key_terms.definition: The rough time frame after a building collapse during which trapped survivors have meaningfully better odds of being found alive; rescue efforts intensify as this deadline approaches.

cards.title: Researchers find a flaw that let weaker AI models leak stronger models' hidden reasoning — and even passwords
cards.what_happened: The researchers found that an encrypted reasoning block created in one session could be **replayed into a different session** and, if handed to a **cheaper, lighter model from the same company**, would sometimes get decoded and printed out in plain text — because lighter models are built with less aggressive filtering than a company's flagship model. Testing this against thousands of publicly logged AI-agent conversations, the team recovered **over 315,000 hidden reasoning blocks**, some of which contained sensitive data like API keys and passwords that had leaked into a model's internal reasoning. The three companies have since updated how they handle this: **Anthropic** now says reasoning blocks are tied to the specific model that created them and should be discarded when switching models; **Google** says its backend manages compatibility automatically; **OpenAI** still instructs developers to replay reasoning blocks manually.
key_points: Security researchers showed **OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google's** AI systems could be tricked into revealing their **encrypted internal "reasoning"** — normally hidden from users.
The trick: replaying a hidden-reasoning block from one session into **a weaker model** in the same family, which lacks the safety filtering to refuse and just prints it out.
Across **6,708 public AI-agent conversation logs**, researchers decoded **315,320 hidden reasoning blocks**, some containing **leaked API keys and passwords**.

The flaw enables **four types of abuse**: stealing reasoning to copy a rival's model, extracting private user data, uncovering content models were told to hide, and smuggling hidden instructions past safety checks.
cards.moot: Any system that must pass "private" internal data between separate calls or sessions creates a seam where that data can leak — encryption alone doesn't help if the receiving side can be tricked into decoding it for you.

depth.background: Modern AI "reasoning" models think through a problem in a hidden scratchpad before giving their final answer — a technique that improves accuracy but that companies keep encrypted and invisible to protect their trade secrets and prevent misuse. Developers who build tools on top of these models sometimes need to pass that hidden reasoning between separate API calls to keep a conversation coherent, which is where this flaw lived. A research team published a paper titled "Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLM APIs" documenting how they exploited this.
depth.why_it_matters: AI companies spend enormous sums building the "reasoning" ability into their models and treat how it works as a competitive secret — this flaw showed that secret wasn't as protected as assumed, and that ordinary developer conversation logs could contain leaked passwords without anyone realizing it.
depth.ripple_effects: Companies building on these AI APIs need to check whether their own logs of past conversations expose secrets, and AI vendors face pressure to close similar gaps as reasoning models become standard across the industry. It also renews scrutiny on how much AI companies can genuinely keep proprietary as rivals get better at extracting it.
depth.why_now: The vulnerability was published this week as researchers disclosed the paper and vendors began responding with documentation and behavior changes.
depth.watch_next: Whether OpenAI follows Anthropic and Google in changing how encrypted reasoning is handled across model switches, and whether any real-world leaked credentials are confirmed to have caused harm.

key_terms.definition: The hidden step-by-step "thinking" an AI model does internally before giving its final answer — normally not shown to the user.
Training a smaller, cheaper AI model to copy a larger one's behavior — something companies try to prevent rivals from doing to their proprietary models.

prev_ref.title: India's rupee slides to fresh lows and oil firms bleed ₹1,000 crore a day as the Strait of Hormuz

cards.title: US-Iran talks on reopening the Strait of Hormuz break down, and oil prices rise on the deadlock
cards.what_happened: Iran told mediators that a technical agreement with Oman on strait management **would not be enough on its own** — Tehran is now also demanding the US ease sanctions and pay war reparations before it will let normal shipping resume. Talks stalled as a result, and **oil prices rose** on the fading odds of a quick resolution: Brent crude settled near **$89 a barrel** and US crude (WTI) near **$83**. Iran's Supreme Leader Khamenei's son and de facto successor, Mojtaba Khamenei, named a new military high command, including Ali Abdollahi as armed forces chief of staff. Trump reiterated that the US would not tolerate interference with shipping, while Gulf states have grown visibly frustrated at being caught between the two sides.
key_points: Oil prices climbed after **Iran added new demands** — including eased US sanctions and **war reparations** — before it will reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

The strait normally carries about **one-fifth of the world's oil supply**; shipping through it has collapsed to **8–15 vessels crossing on Aug 4–6**, versus roughly **130 transits before the conflict**.
Iran's Supreme Leader reshuffled the country's **top military leadership**, naming new armed forces and Revolutionary Guard commanders.
President Trump said the US has **"total control"** of the strait and warned Iran would **"get blown away"** if it interfered with shipping there.
cards.moot: Chokepoints — narrow physical passages that a large share of global trade must funnel through — give small players outsized leverage over prices everyone pays, because disrupting the passage is far cheaper than the economic damage it causes downstream.

thread.previously: Yesterday's coverage focused on the rupee and Indian oil companies bleeding money as the strait stayed shut, with a deal seen as unlikely soon.
thread.changed: Today the block is explicitly on the diplomatic track: Iran has added new demands (sanctions relief, reparations) that talks with Oman alone can't satisfy, oil prices have ticked up in response, and Iran has also reshuffled its military command.

depth.background: Since a US-Israel-Iran war erupted in late February 2026, Iranian attacks on shipping and US retaliatory strikes have repeatedly disrupted the **Strait of Hormuz**, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that oil tankers must pass through to leave the Gulf. Periodic ceasefire efforts and partial truces have not held, and Trump has followed a pattern of threatening major new strikes and then pulling back. Earlier in August, Iran appeared close to a deal with Oman on managing traffic through the strait, which briefly lifted hopes of it reopening.
depth.why_it_matters: Around a fifth of the world's traded oil normally passes through this one chokepoint, so a prolonged closure keeps a floor under global oil and fuel prices — raising costs for households and businesses far from the Middle East. It also shows how close a full ceasefire can look, then unravel, when each side keeps adding new conditions.
depth.ripple_effects: Higher and more volatile oil prices feed into inflation readings worldwide, complicating central banks' interest-rate decisions (including the US Federal Reserve's, due mid-September). Countries that import most of their oil, including India, face a bigger import bill and pressure on their currencies — India's rupee has already been sliding partly because of this same standoff.
depth.why_now: The breakdown follows days of cautious optimism after Iran signaled a deal with Oman was close; adding fresh demands on sanctions and reparations shows Tehran is using the leverage of continued disruption rather than settling quickly.
depth.watch_next: Whether Saudi Arabia's diplomatic push — Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has urged Trump to hold off on further strikes — produces a new round of talks before shipping losses deepen further.
depth.market_link: Crude oil (Brent/WTI), airline and shipping stocks, and oil-import-dependent currencies like the Indian rupee are directly exposed to how long the strait stays disrupted.

key_terms.definition: A narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman that nearly all oil shipped out of the Gulf must sail through — a natural chokepoint for the global oil trade.
The two most widely quoted oil price benchmarks — Brent for oil traded internationally, WTI (West Texas Intermediate) for US oil.

cards.title: A derecho and flash floods kill at least two and cut power to 800,000 across the US Midwest
cards.what_happened: A **derecho** swept across the Midwest and Ohio Valley on **August 11**, spawning at least **six tornadoes**, including three confirmed EF1s in Iowa and three in the Chicago area. Wind gusts reached **160 km/h (99 mph)** at Gary, Indiana, and the storm knocked out power to more than **800,000 customers** across Illinois, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky, killing at least **two people**. Overnight, the same system dumped as much as **10 inches (25cm) of rain** on south-central Indiana, and the National Weather Service issued flood warnings for multiple rivers as water levels rose toward major flood stage. Areas near New Castle and Connersville, Indiana, saw close to 10 inches of rain in under 24 hours. Flash flooding swamped homes, vehicles and roads across central Indiana on August 12, with more storms and heavy rain forecast into the evening.
key_points: A **derecho** — a fast-moving line of destructive thunderstorms — tore across the Midwest and Ohio Valley on **August 11**, killing at least **two people**.
More than **800,000 homes and businesses** lost power across Illinois, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky.
Winds hit **160 km/h (99 mph)** at Gary, Indiana; at least **six tornadoes** were confirmed or suspected, including three in the Chicago area.
Up to **10 inches (25cm) of rain** fell in south-central Indiana overnight, and forecasters warned of **major river flooding** into Wednesday night.
Flash flood warnings remained active across Indiana on August 12 as rivers continued rising.
cards.moot: A single storm system can combine tornado-strength winds with flash-flood rainfall, which is why a 'severe thunderstorm' warning can sometimes be as dangerous as a tornado warning — the total damage footprint of a derecho is often far larger.

depth.background: Derechos are a known but under-the-radar hazard in the US Midwest and Great Plains — long-lived, straight-line windstorms that can damage areas hundreds of miles wide in a single afternoon, unlike a tornado, which is narrow and short-lived. They form when a cluster of thunderstorms organizes around a strong pocket of falling cold air that fans out and accelerates along the ground. **August is peak season** for this kind of storm complex in the Ohio Valley, where warm, humid summer air collides with cooler fronts dropping south from Canada. The region has also had an unusually wet, hot summer, priming rivers and soil for flash flooding when a storm dumps a huge volume of rain in a few hours.
depth.why_it_matters: Derechos combine tornado-speed winds with flash-flood-level rainfall over a much bigger area than a typical storm, which is why they cause disproportionate damage and prolonged outages. Widespread power loss during a hot mid-August week also raises health risks — no air conditioning, spoiled food, disrupted water treatment — for hundreds of thousands of people.
depth.ripple_effects: Insurers face a fresh round of storm-damage claims across four states, and utilities in Illinois, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky face days of repair work before power is fully restored. Flooded roads and rail lines can disrupt Midwest freight and agricultural logistics — Indiana and Ohio are major corn- and soybean-growing states — right as crops approach a critical late-summer growth stage.
depth.why_now: This is the tail of a very active, wet North American summer; a cold front dropping south from Canada collided with unusually warm, moisture-laden air over the Ohio Valley, fueling both the derecho's winds and the flash flooding that followed.

depth.background: The Consumer Price Index, or **CPI**, is the US government's main measure of how fast the price of everyday goods and services is rising — it's what people mean when they say 'inflation'. depth.background: Manipur, a northeastern Indian state, has been gripped by ethnic violence between the Meitei and Kuki-Zo communities that erupted in 2023, displacing tens of thousands of people and killing hundreds. The unrest was severe enough that the Supreme Court took the unusual step of directly monitoring relief, rehabilitation, and law-and-order efforts in the state, rather than leaving oversight entirely to the central and state governments. Despite periodic government claims of normalization, displaced families in relief camps and disputed pockets of the state have continued to report unresolved compensation, housing, and security issues.

Beijing does not recognize Arunachal Pradesh at all — it refers to the entire state as **'Zangnan'** and claims it as Chinese territory.

cards.moot: When two countries can't agree on a formal border, small symbolic acts — like what a mountain pass is officially called — become stand-ins for the larger territorial dispute, and both sides use them to signal resolve without escalating to open conflict.

depth.background: Arunachal Pradesh is an Indian state in the country's northeast that China claims in its entirety, calling it 'South Tibet' or 'Zangnan.' The two countries fought a war over their shared Himalayan border in 1962, and the border — known as the **Line of Actual Control** — has never been formally settled, meaning both sides periodically contest small pieces of territory or, as here, contest the names attached to land each already controls on its own side.
